newsitem.title: EGYPT: Sudan's Mahdi does not rule out secession for south.
newsitem.headline: Sudan's Mahdi does not rule out secession for south.

text.p: Ousted Sudanese prime minister Sadeq al-Mahdi said the Sudanese opposition was working for the unity of Sudan but did not rule out secession for the south as a solution to more than a decade of war.

Mahdi told a packed lecture hall at the American University in Cairo on Tuesday night the Islamist goverment of President Omar Hassan al-Bashir, who toppled Mahdi in a coup in 1989, had united the opposition as never before and the conflict in the south would tear Sudan apart if it lasted any longer.
Asked if he thought secession for the mainly Christian and animist region was the answer, Mahdi declared: "Any alternative is better than war."
He said: "The current Sudanese political forces have given us a blessing in disguise for they have created the negative conditions for pushing the people towards national unity."

The rebel Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), which is now fighting the government with the northern opposition under the umbrella of the National Democratic Alliance, has waged a war for autonomy from the Arabised north for 13 years.

The conflict has drained the resources of one of Africa's poorest nations. But since January, the rebels have branched out in Sudan and say they are fighting in the north and east to topple the government by sparking a popular uprising.

Egypt, Sudan's northern neighbour, has poor ties with the Bashir government but President Hosni Mubarak has repeatedly said that his country is opposed to any division of Sudan. Analysts say Egypt is concerned about its share of Nile water.
Mahdi said he believed that all riparian states would respect the "international nature" of the Nile and that an independent south would do the same.

Mahdi, who heads the opposition Umma party in exile and who was put under house arrest in Khartoum many times but is now based in the Eritrean capital Asmara, also warned countries against investing in Sudan.

"The last thing expected is for anyone to put the resources of Sudan into the hands of this regime. Any individual, company or state that does so is declaring war on the Sudanese people and putting themselves on the blacklist," he said.
"If they invest, they are doing so at their own peril."
Rebels have warned foreign companies that they would "chase them away with guns" if they set up in Sudan.
Sudan hopes to develop its flagging economy with foreign investment. Bashir opened an oilfield in March developed with Qatari partnership.

Canada's Arakis Energy Corp and its Chinese and Malaysian partners in March signed final agreements for their $1 billion oil development project in Sudan to develop three blocks. The deal is for 25 years.
